en: The Ritual for Cultivating the Medicine Buddha’s Mandala Layout, translated and supplemented by Āwaṅ Zhabs, Abbot of Beijing Jingzhu Temple.
There are three parts to the ritual for practicing the Seven Medicine Buddha Sūtras: the preliminary practices, the main body, and the concluding rites.
Regarding the preliminary practices,
as stated in the *Saptabuddha-pūrvapraṇidhāna-mahāguṇa-dhāraṇī-vidhi-sūtra*,
the section on the method for gathering the recitation says:
To those who wish to practice the ritual procedure for paying homage to the Seven Tathāgatas,
they should bathe their bodies and put on fresh, clean garments.
He partakes of pure food,
completely setting aside all defiled afflictions and the like from his mind.
Regarding the benefits of the *Sūtra on the Fundamental Merits of the Triple Gem*,
they will give rise to profound reverence, faith, and understanding,
and will practice the contemplation and cultivation of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
If a practitioner is a householder and observes the fast and precepts,
they should begin on the eighth day of the waxing moon.
In the place where the ritual is performed,
they sweep it clean and set up numerous banners and streamers.
It is used for solemn adornment.
Inside, one constructs a great fragrant maṇḍala,
either with pigments or fine flour.
Alternatively, one may spread flowers and rice upon it and place an image of the Buddha there;
such an image may be cast, painted, or sculpted as appropriate.
It would be even better if there were śarīra relics present.
Furthermore, it includes the seating positions for all worldly and supramundane retinues.
Everything was prepared in accordance with the Dharma;
all those who provided offerings also exerted their utmost efforts in arranging them.
In front of each of the seven Buddhas,
seven lamps were lit,
and seven five-colored banners topped with human heads were suspended.
Furthermore, fragrant flowers, powdered incense, food, medicine, and items such as the seven treasures, the eight auspicious symbols, and jeweled vases were all prepared.
Having thus arranged these offerings,
the great assembly sat upon their secure seats.
Each entered into the meditative concentration of emptiness and,
according to their capacity, recited the *Sūtra on the Merit of the Original Vows of the Seven Buddhas*,
as well as all the vast, profound, and esoteric scriptures such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Thereafter, exert all effort to recite this dhāraṇī ritual manual for a minimum of seven days, or twenty-one days.
Thirty-five days; forty-nine days is even more excellent.
This is stated in other versions of the ritual manual.
I now follow this intent.
Regarding the creation of these ritual manuals,
there are two methods.
First, the method for arranging the altar;
second, the method for cultivation.
Regarding the method for arranging the altar:
In an exceptionally auspicious location, the area above,
below, and in the four cardinal and intermediate directions was purified and adorned;
in its center, a small table was set.
If there is no stand, one may set up a single pure platform;
it is also permissible to smear it with fragrant medicinal substances.
Above it is depicted the incomparable palace,
with four sides and four gates,
excluding the archways.
The layout and ritual protocols of the hall follow strict standards;
although they do not employ the *sūtra*-stringing methods of the Secret Mantra (*Guhyamantra*) division,
the seating arrangements for the eight Mahāyāna deities within the hall are established.
When reaching the curves of the doorway,
it is essential not to lose the proper proportions.
As for the method of dividing the colors:
Within the incomparable palace,
there stands a square platform with three tiers of steps.
The upper layer is white;
the middle and lower layers are blue in the eastern direction.
The south is yellow;
the west is red; the north is green.
On the upper surface of the upper terrace,
place an eight-petaled lotus flower.
On the upper surface of the middle terrace...
Place a sixteen-petaled lotus flower upon the upper surface of the lower pedestal.
Place a twenty-four-petaled lotus flower upon it.
Upon the central platform, the cardinal and intermediate directions, and the lotus petals,
lion thrones are established respectively.
Upon the central platform, moon-disc thrones are established.
Descend from the platform starting at the eastern gate,
circumambulating to the right the ten guardians of the directions as well as the deities of the sun and moon.
All [the deities] are seated upon mountain thrones.
To their left, the twelve yakṣa generals are all seated upon brocade cushions.
Within the four gates, the gods of the Four Great Kings all occupy lotus-moon disc seats;
these are the aforementioned seats.
Alternatively, one may apply pigments to it;
as for the ground outside,
one should spread precious sand over it.
Adorned with flowers such as the *urubaka*,
it was as exquisitely decorated as the most wondrous realm of Sukhāvatī.
Outside, there is a perimeter wall that resembles a mountain of iron encircling it;
atop the wall rises a precious eaves supported by pillars shaped like ascending dou-beams.
It is not like the eaves of a wall in a secret ritual,
nor is it like the Brahma-palaces within a vast garden.
The general meaning should be understood as follows:
although there are many ritual manuals that have been composed,
we now follow the venerable master Asaṅga, a son of the Buddha.
The manner of his attire:
he stands upon the central platform,
on a lion throne made of jewels.
The child rests like the form of Mañjuśrī;
upon it is spread a scroll of scripture,
and atop the scroll sits a case for the Eight Hundred Verse Sūtra.
In the east is Śākyamuni Buddha, yellow in color;
his right hand performs the earth-touching mudrā,
and his left hand performs the samādhi mudrā.
In the south is the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound, yellow in color;
his right hand is in the mudrā of granting boons,
and his left hand is in the mudrā of meditative concentration.
The Tathāgata Aśoka-agra of the western quarter is light red in color;
his two hands form the mudrā of meditative equipoise (samādhi-mudrā).
The Tathāgata Suviśruta-śrī-rāja of the northern quarter is yellow in color.
The right hand performs the *abhaya-mudrā*,
and the left hand performs the *samādhi-mudrā*.
In the northeast corner is the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabharāja, blue in color.

The right hand displays the *varada-mudrā* (gesture of granting boons) and holds an arura fruit— that is, an aśvattha berry; the left hand displays the *samādhi-mudrā* (gesture of meditative concentration),
upon which rests an alms bowl.
In the southeast corner is the Tathāgata Vimalasuvarṇa, yellow in color,
with both hands in the dharmacakra mudrā.
In the southwest corner is the Tathāgata Dharmasāgaragarjitasvara, light red in color.
He forms the *dharmacakra-mudrā* with both hands.
In the northwest corner is the Tathāgata Dharmasāgaravarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña, red in color;
his right hand performs the *vara-mudrā*.
The left hand is in the mudrā of meditative concentration.
These eight Tathāgatas all wear saffron-colored dharma robes.
Adorned with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, he sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
Upon a lotus petal on the central terrace,
he sits facing east.
The form of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is golden-red in color;
his left hand holds a scripture,
and his right hand grasps a sword.
On his right side is the Bodhisattva Jie-duo (Ratnatārā), white in color,
with both hands in the vajra-fist mudrā,
pressing against his two cheeks.
He sits with a subtle air of pride.
In the northeast corner is the Bodhisattva Sunlight-Pervading-Illumination (Sūryaprabhāparyantāvabhāsa), golden-red in color;
his right hand holds an *utpala* flower.
Upon the flower, place a Buddhist scripture;
its upper part is adorned with the mark of a sun disc.
The left hand forms the vajra-fist mudrā.
He presses down upon the crown of the head.
To the left of Mañjuśrī is the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, green in color; his right hand holds a vajra at his chest, and his left hand holds a jewel garland.
In the southeast corner is the Bodhisattva Moonlight Pervasive Illumination (Candraprabha-prabhāsa),
white in color. His right hand holds an *utpala* flower,
upon which rests a Sanskrit manuscript.
The upper [face] is adorned with the crescent-moon mark;
the left hand forms the vajra-fist mudrā,
pressing upon the hip.
Furthermore, regarding the eleven Great Mahāsattva Bodhisattvas as recorded in the preface of this sūtra:
in the south, one should sit upright and visualize the form of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, who is white in color.
He holds a lotus flower in his hand.
To his left is the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, yellow in color,
holding a lotus flower in his hand.
Above, he adorns a single eye.
To his right is Maitreya Bodhisattva, yellow in color,
holding a nāga-flower tree in his hand.
The upper array of the army is the *kamaṇḍalu* (water flask). In the southwest corner is the white Bodhisattva Saṃbhārasambhava, holding a sword in his hand.
In the west, seated upright, is the white Bodhisattva Amoghasiddhi.
He holds a sword in his hand.
To his left is the Bodhisattva Subhūṣaṇā, white in color,
holding a lotus tree in her hand.
Above it, the Dharma-piṭaka is adorned with precious jewels.
To its right is the Bodhisattva Bhāskara-prajñā (P'o-ming-hui), white in color,
holding a staff in his hand.
In the northwest corner is the Bodhisattva Sucintita, white in color,
holding a precious vase.
In the north, seated upright, is the Bodhisattva Merupradīpa, white in color.
Holding a lotus tree in his hand,
it is adorned above with the mark of a crescent moon.
To his left is the Bodhisattva Subhāṣitaghoṣa, light blue in color.
He holds an *utpala* flower in his hand,
adorned above with a vajra and a flaming jewel.
To his right is the yellow Bodhisattva King of the Sumeru Peak.
Holding jeweled tassels in their hands,
these eleven bodhisattvas each form their respective hand-seals with the right hand at the chest.
The left hand forms the vajra-fist mudrā, supporting the hip;
he is adorned with various jewels and wears celestial garments of diverse colors.
Possessing marks of gentleness and goodness,
the Bodhisattva sat cross-legged upon a lotus-petal seat below the platform.
Inside the eastern gate,
in the left row, is the yakṣa general Atibhaya,
yellow in color and holding a mace.
To his right is the Great General Vajrayakṣa,
blue in color and holding a sword;
next is the Great General Ugradākṣa.
The one in the southeast corner is yellow and holds a *daṇḍa*; the Great Yakṣa General holding a star in the northeast corner is light blue and holds a *daṇḍa*.
In the north is the yakṣa general Vāyu-dhara,
red in color and holding a trident;
he dwells in the abode of the yakṣas.
The yakṣa general Dṛḍhabala is smoke-colored and holds a sword;
[the yakṣa] Lohitākṣa is red and holds a mace.
The yakṣa general named Grasping Drink (Gṛhītapāna) is yellow in color and holds a staff;
in the northwest corner is the yakṣa general named Grasping Speech (Gṛhītālāpa).
The western yakṣa general, Dhīmat, is yellow in color and holds a noose.
The yakṣa general Gṛhītacala is blue in color and holds a staff;
the yakṣa general Vṛtta is likewise blue.
Red in color and holding a wheel.
These aforementioned yakṣa generals each form their respective hand-seals (mudrā) at their chests with their right hands.
In their left hands, they all hold precious mice that emit jeweled pearls from their mouths;
they are adorned with various treasures.
Wearing celestial garments,
with a large belly and a corpulent body,
his appearance was fearsome.
They all sit as if playing, like a sovereign;
within the eastern gate, to the right, is the seat upon which the Sun-Deity (Rājasūrya) sits.
A red second-hand [image] holding a solar disc.
To its left, upon a swan seat, is Candraprabha,
the Devaputra of Moonlight.
White in color, holding a moon disc in his hand;
next is Brahmā upon a swan throne,
with four faces and yellow in color.
The right hand holds a wheel;
the left hand holds a precious vase.
In the southeast corner, atop an elephant throne, is the deity Śakra.
The white one holds a vajra.
In the south, on a goat throne, is Agni;
he is red in color and holds a fire-bowl in his hand.
On a buffalo seat is Yama-deva,
blue in color and holding a staff;
on a corpse seat is Rākṣasa-deva.
The Water Deity (Varuṇa) is blue in color, holds a sword,
and sits upon a water-animal throne;
he is white in color and holds a snake-noose with both hands.
In the southwest corner, upon a deer throne, is the Wind Deity,
light blue in color and holding a wind-banner.
In the west, upon a horse throne, is the Yakṣa Deity.
The yellow one holds a *pāśa*;
on a bull seat is Īśvara,
white in color and holding a trident.
The Earth Goddess is seated upon a boar;
she is yellow in color and holds a flask with her two hands.
These are the various deities.
Wearing a jeweled crown and clad in celestial robes,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King of the Eastern Gate,
is white in color and holds a lute with his two hands.
In the southern gate is Virūḍhaka, the Heavenly King of Increase, blue in color and holding a sword.
In the western gate is Virūpākṣa, the Heavenly King of Broad Eyes,
red in color and holding a snake-noose.
At the northern gate is the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa,
yellow in color and holding a jewel-bearing rat.
These are the aforementioned Four Heavenly Kings.
He wears a jeweled crown on his head,
is clad in celestial garments,
and stands with both feet together.
Regarding such characteristics as these,
it does not matter whether they are made of incense, medicine, wood, clay, or modeled in paint;
it is especially excellent if they are fashioned from gold or silver.
It is essential merely to arrange the ritual implements according to the established protocols;
all [participants] should face toward the center.
According to the original ancient texts, there is no mention of painting [the deities].
This is intended for the purpose of providing a practical application.
If no painted image is available,
one should use a maṇḍala according to the aforementioned ritual procedure.
It may also be done with flowers, rice, or cloth.
Although it is taught in this way, one must not form the notion that they are Buddhas;
furthermore, it is essential that the place not be disordered.
One must earnestly hope for the blessings and guidance of the Truthful Ones; thus,
one spontaneously becomes a vast seat,
upon which one invites all Buddhas to descend.
This is not merely to enter into what was previously laid out;
rather, the power of creating seven physical images in accordance with the words of the sutras is truly the essential requirement.
The seven Buddhas, together with their retinues,
likewise manifest by means of this power;
from the wisdom of those who personally invite the assembly of guests to those who pass away into parinirvāṇa.
Nor should one harbor doubts;
it is simply because it has been performed through the power of discernment by those who are wise and virtuous.
Once the placement is complete.
Thereafter, one should arrange the offerings.
Within these offerings,
before each Buddha, [place...]
Light seven lamps for each and suspend seven multi-colored banners;
these constitute the essential offerings.
This is recorded in the "Vow Text for Saving and Delivering Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it involves using various types of incense and medicinal herbs to prepare water of merit.
Scented ointments,
or fresh flowers,
or artificial flowers.
Incense such as candana, agarū, and turuṣka.
Furthermore, there are fragrant offerings made from various types of incense and flour;
food offerings consisting of various kinds of delicious flavors;
and medicinal offerings consisting of various medicines.
Banners, streamers, and robes;
the seven treasures and the eight precious gems.
The eight auspicious objects and other offerings were abundant;
it was especially virtuous to divide them into seven portions for the great yakṣa generals.
Before the various deities, such as the Protectors of the Directions and the Local Deities,
offerings may be omitted; however,
according to the ritual manual of this sūtra, they are now provided.
One should present food offerings,
one portion for each category.
Thereafter, fill the precious *dhāraṇī* vase completely with fragrant medicinal water.
Tie a silk cloth around the neck of the jar and adorn its mouth by inserting fruit branches;
meanwhile, the patron must be reverent and sincere toward the assembly of bhikṣus present at the gathering.
Recite the Eight Hundred Verse Prajñāpāramitā and other profound and esoteric sūtras as auxiliary dharmas.
Although this ritual manual may be practiced at any time,
if it is performed on an auspicious day of the seventh lunar month,
its merit will exceed that of ordinary days by a hundred thousand million times.
What are the seven? First,
the day the Buddha was in the womb was the fifteenth day of the second month of summer in the year Jih-wei.
The day on which the two Buddhas descended was the seventh day of the fourth month in the year Gengshen.
The day on which the three Buddhas left home [to become mendicants]—
It was the eighth day of the late spring of the Wuzi year.
It was the day the four Buddhas attained enlightenment.
It was the fifteenth day of the fourth month of the Jiawu year.
The day the five Buddhas turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park was the fourth day of the sixth month of late summer in the year they attained enlightenment.
It was also the day the six Buddhas returned from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
It was the twenty-second day of the second month of autumn in the Gengzi year,
the anniversary of the Parinirvāṇa of the Seven Buddhas.
It was the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the Gengchen year.
These auspicious dates have been fixed and determined without error. If,
by means of the Dharma Master Sajjawa...
The date of his descent as spoken of was the eighth day of the late spring in the year of Dingmao;
according to the Great Master Pujexi, however.
It is said that his descent was in the year of the Male Wood Horse;
according to the two masters Khache Paṇchen and Chöphurwa Lozang Gyatso.
The date for returning is stated as the twenty-second day of the month of Kṛttikā;
this is the meaning explained by those wise ones.
Profound and secret, it is immeasurable and cannot be fully recounted.
What I have spoken is but a portion thereof.
This is the same for those who practice constantly.
Furthermore, as seen in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other scriptures,
it is said that on the day the Buddha manifested supernatural transformations— the second day of the second month— he attained the realization of Bodhi.
The day of the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma,
and the day of his descent and return—
these four days are auspicious.
For anyone who performs virtuous deeds, the merit is hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater than on ordinary days;
such merit is immeasurable. Second, the method for cultivation is recorded in this very sutra.
The Ritual Manual for the Cultivation of Bhaiṣajyaguru and the Method for Arranging the Maṇḍala is Complete.
